The word sash has two completely separate, unrelated meanings. Both are common, so knowing both is essential.
Meaning 1: A strip of cloth worn on the body

A sash is a long, wide strip of cloth, ribbon, or fabric that a person wears either around their waist or diagonally across their chest (from one shoulder down to the opposite hip). It is almost never worn for warmth or protection — its purpose is almost always decorative, ceremonial, or symbolic. It tells you something about the person wearing it.

Around the waist: Think of a sash as a fancy, soft alternative to a belt. Instead of a rigid buckle, it is fabric — often silky, colorful, or ornate — tied or draped around the waist. A karate student, for example, wears a colored sash (or belt) around the waist that shows their skill level. A bridesmaid's dress might have a satin sash tied in a bow at the back. A traditional Japanese kimono is fastened at the waist with a wide sash called an obi. In all these cases, the sash sits at the waist and is part of the overall outfit.

Across the chest: This is perhaps the most iconic image of a sash. Picture a beauty pageant contestant — Miss World or Miss America — wearing a wide ribbon running from one shoulder diagonally down to the opposite hip, with words like "Miss Universe" printed on it. That is a sash. Military officers and royalty often wear sashes this way too, to indicate their rank, honor, or the organization they represent. When a head of state from one country visits another, they may be presented with a ceremonial sash to wear. When a child is inaugurated as a school captain, they might be given a sash to wear across their chest as a badge of honor.

The key idea: a sash worn on the body is fabric that communicates status, role, achievement, or belonging, and it does so visually and immediately.
Meaning 2: The frame of a window (or door)

This meaning is completely different from the first. A sash is also the movable frame — typically made of wood or metal — that holds the glass panes inside a window. It is not the wall around the window; it is the actual sliding or moving part that contains the glass.

The most familiar example is the sash window (also called a double-hung window), which is extremely common in older British and American homes. If you picture a classic rectangular window that you open by pushing the bottom half upward, what you are pushing is the lower sash. Such a window usually has two sashes stacked on top of each other, both of which can slide up or down independently. Each sash is essentially a wooden (or metal) rectangle filled with glass, sitting inside a track in the window frame, designed to be raised or lowered.

So when a painter or carpenter talks about replacing a sash, they mean replacing the glass-holding frame inside a window — not the surrounding frame embedded in the wall (that outer fixed frame is called the casing or frame), but the inner movable part that actually opens and closes.
How to tell the two meanings apart

Since these two meanings are completely unrelated, context makes it immediately obvious which one is meant:

  • If the word appears alongside people, clothing, ceremonies, or uniforms → it's the fabric worn on the body.
  • If the word appears alongside windows, buildings, carpentry, or construction → it's the window frame.

You will almost never be confused in real life because the contexts are so different.

• Sash (cloth): The beauty queen wearing a ribbon across her chest. The martial artist's belt. The royal officer's ceremonial strip of fabric from shoulder to hip.
  • Sash (window): The sliding wooden frame that holds the glass in an old-style window. When you push up the bottom of a window to let air in, you are lifting the sash.

That is the complete picture of the word "sash" in its noun form — both of its distinct meanings, fully covered.
